This includes methods dedicated to the bipartitioning case [BCR97, KRC00, Fel05, SST03, Arm07, AFHM08, DGRW12, DW12, FW11, HPZ13, HK99, LR03] and some methods that solve the general GPP [FMDS+98, Sen01].
Most of the methods rely on the branch-and-bound framework [LD60].

Bounds are derived using various approaches:
Karisch et al. [KRC00] and Armbruster [Arm07] use semi-definite programming, and Sellman et al. [SST03] and Sensen [Sen01] employ multi-commodity flows.
Linear programming is used by Brunetta et al. [BCR97], Ferreira et al. [FMDS+98], Lisser et al. [LR03] and by Armbruster et al. [AFHM08].
Hager et al. [HPZ13, HK99] formulate GPP in form of a continuous quadratic program on which the branch and bound technique is applied.
The objective of the quadratic program is decomposed into convex and concave components.
The more complicated concave component is then tackled by an SDP relaxation.
Felner et al. [Fel05] and Delling et al. [DGRW12, DW12] utilize combinatorial bounds. Delling et al. [DGRW12, DW12] derive the bounds by computing minimum ss-tt cuts between partial assignments (A,B)(A,B), i. e., A,B⊆VA,B\subseteq V and A∩B=∅A\cap B=\emptyset. The method can partition road networks with more than a million nodes, but
its running time highly depends on the bisection width of the graph.

In general, depending on the method used, two alternatives can be observed. Either the bounds derived are very good and yield
small branch-and-bound trees but are hard to compute. Or the bounds are somewhat weaker and yield larger trees but are faster
to compute. The latter is the case when using combinatorial bounds.
On finite connected subgraphs of the two dimensional grid without holes, the bipartitioning problem can be solved optimally in O⁡(n4)\mathrm{O}\!\left(n^{4}\right) time [FW11].
Recent work by Bevern et al. [vBFSS13] looks at the parameterized complexity for computing balanced partitions in graphs.

All of these methods can typically solve only very small problems while having very large running times, or if they can solve large bipartitioning instances using a moderate amount of time [DGRW12, DW12], highly depend on the bisection width of the graph.
Methods that solve the general GPP [FMDS+98, Sen01] have immense running times for graphs with up to a few hundred nodes. Moreover, the experimental evaluation of these methods only considers small block numbers k≤4k\leq 4.

4.2 Spectral Partitioning

One of the first methods to split a graph into two blocks, spectral bisection, is still in use today.
Spectral techniques were first used by Donath and Hoffman [DH72, DH73] and Fiedler [Fie75], and have been improved subsequently by others [Bop87, PSL90, Sim91, HL95b, BS93].
Spectral bisection infers global information of the connectivity of a graph by computing the eigenvector corresponding to the second smallest eigenvalue of the Laplacian matrix LL of the graph.
This eigenvector z2z_{2} is also known as Fiedler vector; it is the solution of a relaxed integer program
for cut optimization.
A partition is derived by determining the median value m¯\overline{m} in z2z_{2} and
assigning all nodes with an entry smaller or equal to m¯\overline{m} to V1V_{1} and all others to V2V_{2}.

The second eigenvector can be computed using a modified Lanczos algorithm [Lan50].
However, this method is expensive in terms of running time.
Barnard and Simon [BS93] use a multilevel method to obtain a fast approximation of the Fiedler vector.
The algorithmic structure is similar to the multilevel method explained in Section 6,
but their method coarsens with independent node sets and performs local improvement with Rayleigh quotient iteration.
Hendrickson and Leland [HL95b] extend the spectral method to partition a graph into more than two blocks by using multiple eigenvectors; these eigenvectors are computationally inexpensive to obtain.
The method produces better partitions than recursive bisection, but is only useful for the partitioning of a graph into four or eight blocks.
The authors also extended the method to graphs with node and edge weights.

4.3 Graph Growing

A very simple approach for obtaining a bisection of a graph is called graph growing [KK98a, GL81]. Most of its variants are based on breadth-first search.
Its simplest version works as follows. Starting from a random node vv, the nodes are assigned to block V1V_{1} using a breadth-first search (BFS) starting at vv. The search is stopped after half of the original node weights are assigned to this block and V2V_{2} is set to V\V1V\backslash V_{1}.
This method can be combined with a local search algorithm to improve the partition. Multiple restarts of the algorithm are important to get a good solution.
One can also try to find a good starting node by looking at a node that has maximal distance from a random seed node [GL81].
Variations of the algorithm always add the node to the block that results in the smallest increase in the cut [KK98a].
An extension to k>2k>2 blocks and with iterative improvement is described in Section 5.5.

4.4 Flows

The well-known max-flow min-cut theorem [FF56] can be used to separate two node sets in a graph by computing a maximum flow and hence a minimum cut between them. This approach completely ignores balance, and it is not obvious how to apply it to the balanced GPP.
However, at least for random regular graphs with small bisection width this can be done [BCLS87].
Maximum flows are also often used as a subroutine.
Refer to Section 5.4 for applications to improve a partition
and to Section 6.4 for coarsening in the context of the multilevel framework. There are also applications
of flow computations when quality is measured by expansion or conductance [LR04, AL08].

4.5 Geometric Partitioning

Partitioning can utilize the coordinates of the graph nodes in space, if available.
This is especially useful in finite element models and other geometrically-defined graphs from traditional scientific computing.
Here, geometrically “compact” regions often correspond to graph blocks
with small cut.
Partitioning using nodal coordinates
comes in many flavors, such as recursive coordinate bisection (RCB) [Sim91] and inertial
partitioning [Wil91, FL93]. In each step of its recursion,
RCB projects graph nodes
onto the coordinate axis with the longest expansion of the domain
and bisects them through the median of their projections.
The bisecting plane is orthogonal to the coordinate axis, which can create
partitions with large separators in case of meshes with skewed dimensions. Inertial partitioning can be interpreted as an improvement over
RCB in terms of worst case performance because its bisecting plane is orthogonal to a plane L that minimizes the moments of inertia of nodes. In other words, the projection plane L is chosen such that it minimizes the sum of squared distances to all nodes.

The random spheres algorithm of Miller et al. [MTV91, GMT98] generalizes the RCB algorithm by stereographically projecting the dd dimensional nodes to a random d+1d+1 dimensional sphere which is bisected by a plane through its center point. This method gives performance guarantees for planar graphs, kk-nearest neighbor graphs, and other “well-behaved” graphs.

Other representatives of geometry-based partitioning algorithms are space-filling
curves [PB94, HW02, Zum03, Bad13] which reduce dd-dimensional partitioning to the one-dimensional case.
Space filling curves define a bijective
mapping from VV to {1,…,|V|}\{1,\dots,|V|\}. This mapping aims at the
preservation of the nodes’ locality in space. The partitioning itself is simpler and cheaper than RCB once the
bijective mapping is constructed.
A generalization of space-filling curves to general graphs can be done by so-called graph-filling
curves [SW04].

A recent work attempts to bring information on the graph structure into the geometry by embedding arbitrary graphs into the coordinate space using a multilevel
graph drawing algorithm [KR13].
